baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Chatterjee questions derivative national models and the exclusions of nationalist history
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Targets imperial knowledge and nationalist universalism; not every national history makes the same claims. The checked 1993 chapter supplies a specific argument alongside the broader inherited claim.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Anderson’s account becomes a named interlocutor for Chatterjee’s argument about colonial difference
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Chatterjee is a critic and theorist in his own right; postcolonial accounts do not simply extend Anderson. Chatterjee’s primary 1993 pp. 4–7 praise aspects of Anderson while explicitly disputing modular derivation. A new reverse critique records that productive disagreement.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Chatterjee challenges the modular account associated with Anderson through colonial historical difference
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary pp. 4–7 formulate the objection while retaining print and language as relevant resources. The critique is not a rejection of all national imagining.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Chatterjee extends the Subaltern critique from nationalist historiography to nationalist thought as a 'derivative discourse' (1986)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Guha's 1982 statement (read) opened the critique of elite historiography; his own critique is the separate edge from his person entry. This edge records the distinct extension to nationalist thought. Sarkar (1997, pp. 91–92, read), a former member, traces how Partha Chatterjee's Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986) carried the critique to the colonized intelligentsia's 'derivative discourses', and objects that 'A project that had started with a trenchant attack on elite nationalist historiography had now chosen as its hero the principal iconic figure of official Indian nationalism' (p. 92). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000, p. 25) writes that Chatterjee's book 'extended Guha's criticisms of nationalist historiography into a full-blown, brilliant critique of nationalist thought itself'. The arrow does not claim a denial of all national histories.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Partha Chatterjee’s 1993 intervention challenges Anderson’s modular derivation of colonized nationalisms and foregrounds autonomous cultural imagining in colonial Bengal.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Specifically named critic, primary The Nation and Its Fragments pp. 4–7 freshly reread in rotated scan/OCR. Chatterjee acknowledges the print-capitalism insight while contesting derivative national models; material/spiritual distinction remains his historically situated claim.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Braids a local imperial narrative with the history of governing concepts and practices
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The 2012 interview at 2–3 explains how Fort William and the Black Hole story connect with selectively traced political economy, law and techniques of imperial power. Chatterjee explicitly notes that selection was necessary; no exhaustive global history is inferred.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Brings popular cultural practices into the historical analysis of imperial power
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: At 2, Chatterjee says he learned through Subaltern Studies to interrogate popular culture theoretically. Theatre and football enter alongside policy and elite discourse. His sweeping claim about what other intellectual historians omit is not adopted.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: A comparison of the positions juxtaposed in The New Imperial Histories Reader contrasts Pagden’s rejection of an American-empire label with Chatterjee’s argument that the new global order is imperial.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: An editorial teaching comparison grounded in Barbara Bush’s 2010 substantive review, which explicitly identifies these opposed positions in the reader’s final section. Stephen Howe is the reader’s editor. The comparison is undirected: it does not assert a personal reply, direct encounter, influence, or agreement across every definition of empire. The two original contributions and the complete reader were not freshly read; the positions remain attributed to Bush’s account of their juxtaposition.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: A critique from within: the collective's recovery of subaltern consciousness read as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', and woman shown to be 'the neglected syntagm' of its accounts of insurgency (1985–88); the subaltern later reformulated as those 'removed from lines of social mobility' (2004)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’, Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363, read in full: the group ‘offers a theory of change’, plotting change ‘as confrontations rather than transition’ (p. 330); its practice is ‘closer to deconstruction’ than its self-description (p. 332); ‘This is why I hope to align them with deconstruction’ (p. 336). ‘Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain’ (p. 341), she reads the project to retrieve subaltern consciousness ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’ (p. 342), which ‘would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness’ (p. 356). On gender: ‘The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women’, but ‘I think they overlook how important the concept-metaphor woman is to the functioning of their discourse’ (p. 356); ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357); ‘Male subaltern and historian are here united in the common assumption that the procreative sex is a species apart’ (p. 358); ‘woman is the neglected syntagm of the semiosis of subalternity of insurgency’ (p. 359); ‘if the question of female subaltern consciousness ... is a red herring, the question of subaltern consciousness as such must be judged a red herring as well’ (p. 360). She qualifies: ‘The making-visible of the figure of woman is perhaps not a task that the group should fairly be asked to perform’, but ‘a feminist historian of the subaltern must raise the question of woman as a structural rather than marginal issue’ (p. 361). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha’s ‘autonomous domain’, ‘I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy’ (p. 79; this disagreement with Guha is drawn as its own person-to-person critique, Spivak → Guha, in this revision, and is no longer named in this edge's relationship); ‘the colonized subaltern subject is irretrievably heterogeneous’ (p. 79); ‘If, in the context of colonial production, the subaltern has no history and cannot speak, the subaltern as female is even more deeply in shadow’ (pp. 82–83). In-period readings from historians of the field: Rosalind O’Hanlon, ‘Recovering the Subject’ (Modern Asian Studies, 1988; Verso reprint, read), takes up her phrase (p. 80, citing SS IV p. 342) but warns ‘we should certainly hesitate before accepting Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s suggestion that the strategy of the Subaltern series “in claiming a positive subject-position for the subaltern might be re-inscribed as a strategy for our times”’ (p. 105, citing SS IV p. 345). Gyanendra Pandey, a member, reads the 1988 close as Gramsci’s point: ‘“The subaltern cannot speak,” writes Gayatri Spivak, making, I suggest, much the same point’ (Ethnos, 1995; reprint p. 285, read). Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that the 1988 essay ‘brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies’ and ‘may have provided a major impetus’ for the gender and voice themes of Subaltern Studies IX (1996). Her own later account (‘The New Subaltern’, 2000, read): ‘Except in the work of Susie Tharu ... Subaltern Studies is not informed by feminist theory as such’ (p. 325), and of 1985, ‘Subaltern Studies had no need of such apologetics. But the theoretically inclined metropolitan identitarians did’ (p. 332). Later reading, labelled: Partha Chatterjee (2010; Morris volume, unpaginated) recalls first reading both essays in 1985 with ‘bewilderment’ and calls her intervention ‘the poststructuralist moment in Subaltern Studies’, adding that a changed political context also drove the shift. A critique from within, not a rejection: she joined the editorial collective in the 1990s. edge_389 (gender → subaltern) carries the same story under the gender entry; see the proposed relabel. Guha’s person edge (pe137_guha_rel_01, guha draft) cites the same 1985 essay as reception; this edge is hers. Later reformulation and reading, added in revision 1.151 and dated after 2000: in "Righting Wrongs" (South Atlantic Quarterly, 2004; read in part, from a February 2001 lecture) she writes, "By subaltern I mean those removed from lines of social mobility" (p. 531), and warns that leaders from the domestic "below" ignore "the historically established discontinuity between themselves and the subaltern" (p. 535). Richard M. Eaton (Journal of World History, 2000, read p. 60) summarises the 1985 essay as criticism of "subalternist historians" for "positivist methodologies" (see the truthdebate critique).
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Strategic essentialism and the gendered subaltern, 1985–2004

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Derrida's deconstruction, which she translated and introduced (1976), used and tested as a method for reading colonial texts and subaltern historiography, without being celebrated 'as feminism as such' (1976–88)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period texts. Translator’s preface to Of Grammatology (1976; read at p. lxxvii of the 1997 corrected edition): ‘To locate the promising marginal text, to disclose the undecidable moment, to pry it loose with the positive lever of the signifier; to reverse the resident hierarchy, only to displace it; to dismantle in order to reconstitute what is always already inscribed. Deconstruction in a nutshell. But take away the assurance of the text’s authority, the critic’s control, and the primacy of meaning, and the possession of this formula does not guarantee much.’ Subaltern Studies IV (1985): ‘This is the greatest gift of deconstruction: to question the authority of the investigating subject without paralysing him, persistently transforming conditions of impossibility into possibility’ (p. 336). ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (1985) sets ‘the lessons of deconstruction’ aside for the essay, choosing to ‘strategically take shelter in an essentialism’ (p. 244). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): ‘Derrida is hard to read; his real object of investigation is classical philosophy. Yet he is less dangerous when understood than the first-world intellectual masquerading as the absent nonrepresenter who lets the oppressed speak for themselves’ (p. 87); reading ‘Of grammatology as a positive science’, she reads him as placing the ethnocentric constitution of the Other as ‘Not a general problem, but a European problem’, and ‘As a postcolonial intellectual, I am not troubled that he does not lead me ... to the specific path that such a critique makes necessary’ (p. 89); ‘I have attempted to use and go beyond Derridean deconstruction, which I do not celebrate as feminism as such’ (p. 104); ‘In a certain way, then, the critique of imperialism is deconstruction as such’ (n. 47, p. 108). In-period reception: Eagleton (1999, read) calls Derrida ‘a consecrated figure for this book, about whom hardly a breath of criticism seems permissible’. Prakash (1992; reprint pp. 224–225, read) quotes her definition of deconstruction as an ‘impossible “no” to a structure, which one critiques, yet inhabits intimately’. Later reading, labelled: Chatterjee (2010) recalls that in 1982 the subalternists ‘did not imagine that Jacques Derrida ... could have anything remotely to do with Indian peasants’. Wikidata’s ‘influenced by’ (P737) lists Paul de Man, not Derrida; that is a Wikidata statement, not evidence here. Her translation’s publication dates (first American edition 1976, corrected 1997) are already checked on derrida_grammatology_corrected. edge_025 (derrida → post) tells her story under the group entry; see the proposed relabel.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Vivek Chibber: Dominance without Hegemony rests on “a highly mythologized story” of the English and French bourgeois revolutions, so its contrast between India’s bourgeoisie and Europe’s fails (2013–14); Sewell and Steinmetz accept the critique of Guha’s Europe, while Chatterjee, as Chibber reports him, denies that Guha made claims about those revolutions
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: A named critic without a node, drawn from comparative historical sociology because his case is a comparison of the European bourgeois revolutions with Indian independence, and because his readers here include historical sociologists (Sewell is already a critic on this roster). Chibber's own words, read in part: Guha's work is "foundational for the entire Subalternist project" and "fundamentally flawed", because its "contrastive claims about the Indian bourgeoisie and Indian capitalism ... rest on a comparison with the European achievement", and "Guha quite dramatically misunderstands the European story" (response to Chatterjee, Verso, 25 February 2014); Guha's break between the bourgeoisies of West and East "flows from a highly mythologized story about the great Bourgeois revolutions, one that was rejected decades ago by historians" (JWSR 20:2, 2014, p. 313). Guha's words appear only as Chibber quotes them (Dominance without Hegemony, p. 19: the bourgeoisie's "historic triumphs in England in 1648 and France in 1789"; p. 5). Readers in the JWSR symposium: William H. Sewell Jr. (pp. 300–303, read in full) calls Guha's portrayal of the two revolutions "standard-issue orthodox Marxism—and ... well past its 'sell-by' date" (p. 301) while finding Chibber's own history "a bit shaky"; George Steinmetz (p. 284) writes that "Guha was relying on a version of Marxist political theory and German history that was demolished by the critics of the Sonderweg thesis"; Bruce Cumings finds the critique "persuasive, at least at the level of how one defines hegemony" (p. 290) but says "I don't know Guha's work" (p. 292), so Chibber's claim that all the critics accepted his reading of Guha (p. 313) is not adopted here. The defence: at the Historical Materialism conference (New York, April 2013) and in a written reply, Partha Chatterjee argued, as Chibber reports him, that Guha made no claims about the classic bourgeois revolutions and criticised only the historiography of colonial India; Chatterjee's text is unread. Chibber's book (Postcolonial Theory and the Specter of Capital, Verso, 2013) is unread; its focus on Guha and Chakrabarty is from Hung's introduction (p. 281). The endpoint locates the intervention; it does not make the critique the field's verdict.
